purpose: Rosenthal threat-and-disclosure register (Rosenthal et al., D-Lib Magazine 2005; Marathon R8 Tier A): one row per Rosenthal threat class, mapping it to this wiki's stated strategy and the script/register that evidences it. A threat with no stated strategy is a GAP: its strategy and evidence stay blank and scripts/wiki_threat_register.py lists it as a finding on every check. Nothing is auto-remediated.

strategy: The corpus is plain text under version control and can be exported as checksummed BagIt bags, so the failure of any one storage medium loses no content that another copy cannot reconstitute byte-for-byte.

No single machine is the corpus: the tree is a git working copy whose heads are bound into signed checkpoints, and restore is a checked procedure, not a hope — a dead machine is replaced by re-cloning and verifying against the checkpoint record.
All tooling is stdlib-only Python over plain Markdown and JSONL; no proprietary runtime or database holds the corpus, and the validator re-checks the whole tree with nothing but Python.
Formats are open text (Markdown, JSONL, JSON) and format risk is watched on a register, so a format's decline surfaces as a finding while migration is still cheap, instead of as a loss.

Destructive operations are dry-run by default and retirements leave tombstones instead of deletions; registers are append-only, so an operator's mistake is a new line on the record, never a silent rewrite of history.
Checkpoints binding the tree head are signed and witnessed by a copy kept outside the repository, so a disaster that takes the working tree still leaves a verifiable record of what the corpus was.

Checkpoints are signed against an allowed-signers file and citations are locked by hash in the citation lockfile, so tampering with content or history is detectable against records the attacker would also have to forge.
